items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
items.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
items.summary: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

items.title: Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

By leveraging agentic Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and asynchronous vLLM rollouts, the approach significantly improves complex reasoning and tool compliance in interactive environments.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics

Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences

Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide

Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: What is useFetch in React?
items.summary: useFetch is a Custom Hook in React. It is used to fetch data from an API and reuse the fetching logic in multiple components. Let's fetch user data from an API. Create useFetch.js: import { useState, useEffect } from "react"; function useFetch(url) { useEffect(() => { async function fetchData() { try { setLoading(true); const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Something went wrong"); } const result = await response.json(); setData(result); } catch (err) { setError(err.message); } finally { setLoading(false); } } fetchData(); }, [url]); return { data, loading, error }; } export default useFetch; Use the Custom Hook in App.jsx: import React from "react"; function App() { const { data, loading, error } = useFetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users"); if (loading) { return Loading... ; } if (error) { return Error: {error} ; } return ( User Details {data.map((user) => ( {user.name} {user.email} ))} ); } export default App;

items.summary: Every tax season, millions of people try to hide their Social Security Number or account balance on a PDF by drawing a black rectangle in Preview or an online PDF editor. The problem? A black rectangle is just an annotation sitting on top of the text layer. Anyone who receives that PDF can press Ctrl+A, copy, and paste the "redacted" SSN straight into Notepad. Even worse, most web-based redaction tools require you to upload your unredacted W-2, paystub, or legal contract to their servers first. When building SafePDFRedact, I wanted two guarantees: Zero network uploads (the tool keeps working even if you turn off Wi-Fi). Irreversible redaction (zero recoverable text layer and zero leftover PDF metadata). Both manual drag boxes and client-side regex auto-detections (SSNs, EINs, bank account numbers, emails, phone numbers) are painted directly onto the 2D canvas context. items.title: SQL Server DATETIME vs DATETIME2: Which to Use, and What Converting an Existing Column Costs
items.summary: Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples. TL;DR: Use DATETIME2(3) for new columns: it keeps exact milliseconds in 7 bytes, while DATETIME rounds to steps of 1/300 second in 8. Converting an existing column means dropping its default and indexes first, then a rewrite of every row under a schema lock, about 1.4 seconds and 106 MB of log on one million rows in our test. Pick a precision of 3 or more, or the conversion rounds stored values without an error. For a new SQL Server column, use DATETIME2(3): it keeps exact milliseconds in 7 bytes, where DATETIME rounds every value to a step of 1/300 second and takes 8. The harder question is the column you already have. Converting DATETIME to DATETIME2 is safe for the data at a precision of 3 or more, but the ALTER COLUMN is refused until its default and indexes are gone, then rewrites every row under a lock that blocks reads unless it runs online, and a precision below 3 rounds stored values without a word. items.title: Review the MeowShield config diff, not the obfuscated output diff
items.summary: Disclosure: I help promote MeowShield. Teams that add an obfuscation step to their release usually discover a code-review problem within a week: someone commits a protected bundle, the pull request shows a 40,000-line diff of unreadable characters, and reviewers either rubber-stamp it or give up. Here is a cleaner arrangement. Protected output is a build artifact. Treat it like minified bundles: generate it in CI, store it as a release artifact, and keep it out of the repository. Then the only thing a pull request can change about protection is the configuration. Put the options you send to the protection step in one file, for example protect.config.json. For MeowShield's authorized API the documented request has sourceCode, apiToken and an options object whose mode is low, medium or high. The token comes from a CI secret, never from the file. Copy the full current options shape from the official API docs rather than from memory. A change then reads like this in review: { - "mode": "low", + "mode": "medium", "low": { "renameVariables": "...", "preprocessToES5": true } } That is a one-line diff a human can reason about. Why this change? Link the threat or the bug that motivated it.

items.title: Tenant Cohort Telemetry: Bounding Retention for HTTP Health Checks and Polling
items.summary: For a B2B SaaS experiment across tenant cohorts, begin with a small HTTP poller and an explicit evidence budget. The storage term to estimate first is observations per day multiplied by bytes per observation and retention days. Assume, for illustration, 200 tenants, three checks per tenant, one check per minute, and 1,000 bytes per stored observation. items.title: Node.js Scheduled Data Cleanup — Cron HTTP Endpoint and Queue Workers
items.summary: A nightly cleanup should be one short cron-triggered HTTP request, followed by bounded queue work whenever deletion might exceed the scheduler's execution window. Do not let cron own the scan or the delete. Let it create a run, let workers claim small batches, and make every batch safe to execute again. That is the delivery guarantee that matters when an edtech weekly digest depends on an accurate active-customer set. TL;DR: use a public HTTP cleanup endpoint for short work; for a larger cleanup, have that endpoint enqueue chunked jobs and return promptly. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. On the measured platform leg, a cron run is capped at 900 seconds, messages must stay below 256KB, delayed delivery cannot exceed seven days, and pausing a schedule does not backfill missed runs. Start with a bounded incident exercise: the weekly digest is due Monday, while Sunday night's cleanup is meant to remove expired course trials from the active-customer query. items.title: Typed State Machines for React Email Verification
items.summary: Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, wait for a message, and let the user continue. In a real product, it is an asynchronous workflow with several ways to get stuck. The UI are not just waiting for a promise. It is waiting for a message that may arrive late, may be unreadable, or may belong to an older attempt. A typed state machine gives the React layer a small, explicit contract for those situations. The usual implementation starts with three booleans: isSending, isWaiting, and hasError. That works until a user clicks resend during polling, changes the address, or opens a verification link in another tab. Then combinations appear that the product never intended to show, such as a success message beside an expired-code error. Instead, model the meaningful states: idle: no address has been submitted sending: the request to create a verification attempt is in progress waiting: the attempt exists and the client is waiting for a matching message verified: the server accepted the code or link expired: the attempt lease ended failed: the user can retry after a recoverable error This rules out accidental combinations. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development. The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We've seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. items.summary: After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation. items.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
items.summary: President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. items.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
items.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." items.title: Saving a Telegram chat's photos and videos in posting order: what I learned building a Windows app
items.summary: I wanted one folder per Telegram group with every photo and video in it, numbered in the order they were posted. Telegram's cache doesn't give you that: files sit in folders by type, with names like 5229911934_y.jpg. Telegram Desktop's "Export chat history" is closer, but it's a one-off copy split into photos/ and video_files/, and you have to export again to pick up new posts. So I built Chat Media Collector, a small Windows app that does exactly that. You pick a chat, it shows how many photos and videos there are and how much space they need, and it saves them as 0001.jpg, 0002.mp4, 0003.jpg… Run it again next week and only the new posts are added, with the next numbers. This post is about the parts that turned out more interesting to build than I expected. .NET 8 and WPF: one window, plus a tray icon for scheduled syncs WTelegramClient for Telegram's MTProto API. It's pure C#, so there's no native TDLib to ship. QRCoder for the "scan this with Telegram on your phone" sign-in An MSIX package for the Microsoft Store The core promise is that 0041.jpg is the 41st photo or video in the chat, today and after every later run. items.title: Simplifying modular monolith composition in .NET
items.summary: A layered .NET application splits code by technical role: endpoints in one project, handlers in another, the domain model and data access in their own. Adding a field to an order touches all four. Vertical slices split the same code by feature. Everything orders needs, from the endpoint to the query, sits together, and the change stays in one place. A modular monolith groups slices into modules and puts boundaries between them that a build can check. Orders may call billing through billing's public contract, but not read its tables or use its internal classes, and an architecture test fails if it tries. It still ships from one codebase, as one application or a handful of processes. Those tests cover the modules and exempt the host. The host references every module, because something has to register them, and it decides which ones each process runs. In every setup I've built, that decision was a side effect of something else: which projects a host referenced, what a mediator found in an assembly, what a shared AddX() helper pulled in, which if branches matched a flag. items.summary: A currency converter is only as reliable as its exchange rate API, and free APIs are not very reliable. Free tiers have monthly limits. Some need a key you have to ship inside the app. Some go down for an afternoon. When that happens, a converter shows a spinner, then an error, and the user deletes the app. Here is the pattern I use in Swap+, my SwiftUI currency and VAT app with 154 currencies. It has three layers: A chain of providers, tried in order, so one failing source is invisible to the user. A short-lived cache, so we don't hit any API more than we need to. An offline floor: the last good rates, or bundled defaults, so the app always opens with numbers. Instead of hard-coding one API, each source is a small config value with a priority: struct APIConfig { let name: String let baseURL: String let apiKey: String // empty for free, keyless sources let priority: Int // lower runs first var requiresKey = false // true for paid providers } The keyless sources are the interesting part. items.title: Best Practices for Protecting Sensitive Information and Building User Trust When Your App Goes to the Background
items.summary: This article is an English version of an article I contributed to the official pamphlet of iOSDC Japan 2026 (iOS Developers Conference Japan 2026). Have you ever thought about what your app should do when it moves to the background? The moment a user leaves your app, iOS saves a snapshot of its screen. If that snapshot shows sensitive information, someone nearby could see it when the user casually opens the App Switcher. iOS also keeps these snapshots on the device. Regular apps can't access them, but they could potentially be extracted from a jailbroken device. Apple's documentation states that apps should remove sensitive information when they enter the background. If you skip this step, users' personal information can be exposed without anyone meaning to. This article collects practical know-how, from choosing an approach to the implementation details, including two things that are easy to miss: the keyboard and permission alerts. Apple's official documentation includes the following guideline: Your app's UI must not contain any sensitive user information, such as passwords or credit card numbers. items.title: A Timer Is Not a Clock: What We Learned Building a Time Tracker for Windows, Mac and Linux
items.summary: Counting seconds sounds like the easiest program in the world. Start a timer, add one every second, show the number. We build TimoDesk, a time tracker for remote teams: a desktop app that tracks time on tasks, takes screenshots at set intervals, measures keyboard and mouse activity, and syncs it all to a web dashboard. After shipping it on three platforms, we can say this with confidence: counting seconds is the hardest part of the whole product. This is our first post here, so instead of a feature tour, here are the lessons that cost us the most to learn. TimoDesk started as a single Electron app. Today it is three: Windows: .NET (WPF) Mac: Swift and SwiftUI Linux: Electron We moved Windows and Mac to native code because a time tracker lives in the background all day. It hooks the keyboard and mouse, captures the screen, and wakes up every second. On those two platforms, native code gave us lower memory use, better system integration and fewer surprises with permissions and sleep. The price is real: every rule about time has to be written three times and has to behave the same way three times. Most of what follows came out of that. Our first version did the obvious thing. items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
items.summary: How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. An abundance of systematically incomplete measurements is unlikely to lead to a comprehensive understanding of many of the complex systems that occur in biology. AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

items.title: Why I Built a 4.1 MB Native macOS Screen Recorder in Swift Instead of Using Electron
items.summary: I record product demos and coding walkthroughs on my Mac almost every day, and I kept running into the same annoying trade-off: macOS built-in capture (⌘⇧5) is instant and lightweight, but has zero live teaching tools — no screen pen, no zoom magnifier, no teleprompter. Heavy studio recorders bundle hundreds of megabytes, spin up the fans, lock basic workflows behind monthly subscriptions, and force you to sit through slow re-encoding exports after every short recording. So I built LeanTake in pure Swift, AppKit, and Apple's ScreenCaptureKit — a 4.1 MB notarized macOS app focused on finishing every demo in a single take. Website & Free DMG: https://leantake.hooosberg.com/ Instead of writing raw intermediate frames and forcing a post-production render queue, LeanTake hardware-encodes directly to .mov in real time. The instant you press Stop (⌃⌥R), the finished file is ready to play or share in Finder. items.title: I stress-tested my Mac media player with 400 Mbps 4K files — here's what happened
items.summary: Specs lie. "Supports 4K" can mean anything from buttery playback to a slideshow with fan noise. So before I called SilkPlayer — my free, native macOS media player — ready, I ran it through the files I actually worry about: the Jellyfish 4K HEVC 10-bit stress files at 120, 200 and 400 Mbps, plus 8K Dolby Vision in Profile 5 and Profile 8.4. The setup is deliberately unglamorous: SilkPlayer 2.0.2, Metal hardware decode, zero-copy to the display. No server, no transcoding, no tricks. The files play straight from local storage. All five passed. The 400 Mbps file — several times the bitrate of a 4K Blu-ray — played smooth. The 8K Dolby Vision Profile 5 file showed the colors right, which is the part most Mac players get wrong: Profile 5 stores its color reshaping data in the RPU metadata, and players that ignore it show purple or washed-out frames. SilkPlayer's Profile 5 pipeline is developed in-house, RPU parsing included. I'm not claiming the player is bulletproof. These five tests cover the decode path only. items.title: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch (6 minute read)

The EchoMotion team is currently developing the technology for use in fitness tracking and exploring the use of the technology in combination with first-person vision on smart glasses to efficiently track the objects that a person handles.

items.summary: The US Commerce Department is closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals to bypass export restrictions on advanced computer chips by renting access to them from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
